doc.title: Carmen Lundy interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, February 15, 2023

chapter: Songwriting and recording Fade to Black
title: The unexpected chord in 'Flowers and Candles'
summary: Rowe asks about the harmony under the line 'innocence has died'; she explains it as emotional accompaniment, with a connection dropout.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: I have to fast forward because if I don’t get some input on you on these songs I won’t sleep tonight. I wanted to ask you a couple of specific things about recent compositions and from “Modern Ancestors” you wrote a song called “Flowers and Candles.”

There’s a line about one minute in, at least the video I watched where you sing a downward melodic phrase and the words are “in a place where innocence has died.” And if my ears are correct when you hit the end of that line you landed on the root of the key you’re in, but the chord did not. The chord was not what the ear was expecting. It might have been down a whole step or it might have been just a thicker chord. And can you recall when you sat and wrote that how did that happen?
You mean with the chord not landing on the tonic?

Yeah, the note landed on the tonic but the chord didn’t go there, it was different and then a few bars later it sort of got where the ear was expecting. I don’t mean to make too much out of this but it certainly perked me up, it made me like do my head like that.

Well if you consider the lyric “had died” okay? So if I said, “In a place where innocence had died.” So it’s like going [sings] “In a place where innocence has died.” So I think that we’re in — there’s something about that emotion or that truth about the morbidity of a thought of innocence dying. What am I saying there? So perhaps that was the interpretation of my accompaniment to suggest something sonically that had to do with that. Do you understand? It’s a sonic interpretation. So to just have a perfectly beautiful major chord would not necessarily incline that emotion. You see what I mean? You understand what I mean? And I don’t recall anything unusual or kind of jarring about it. I’d have to go back and listen, because I haven’t listened to that tune in a while. But I think the accompaniment, I think the gift and the role of the accompaniment is to really support not only the lyric and whatever the music is but the emotional aspects of it too. And I kind of like, you know, Phrygian modal sounds in harmony. They don’t throw my ear. I kind of like that — I’m going to use a kind of a —
I think we may have lost you
Okay I have no idea what that was.
Yeah I lost you — we’ll — in the words of old fashioned, we’ll splice that out.

Okay so it’s funny that we’re talking about this. And so yeah, I think that whatever that is you’re hearing, I’m trying to hear, because my brother is playing, Curtis is on bass on that tune and he’s playing the fifth. He’s sort of like on the pedal tone [sings] “And the little boy asks his papa.” So I’m sort of on a major and minor thing anyway so I’ll have to listen again because I’m not really sure exactly —

Yes, and I wouldn’t call it jarring, I would call it, once I heard it the second time I said that’s highly appropriate, what you did there. And so, the other thing, I’d also like to ask you about “Ain’t I Human.”
